questions.text: A standard residential entry door on a floor plan is typically dimensioned at a width of:

rationale.a: Incorrect—0.75 m is too narrow for residential entry; might be used for closets.
rationale.b: Incorrect—0.8 m is below minimum per code.
rationale.d: Incorrect—1.1 m exceeds standard residential; might be commercial double doors.
rationale.correct: Standard residential entry door minimum = 0.80 m clear opening width per PD 1096 Rule VIII Sec 808. Accessible doors require 1.0 m (1000mm). A 0.9m door is typical for bedrooms, bathrooms, residential entries.
rationale.takeaway: Standard residential entry = 0.9 m clear width. Accessible = 1.0 m. Interior doors (bedrooms, bathrooms) can be 0.8m–0.9m depending on code and practice.

questions.text: A floor plan for a multi-story residential building shows a fire-rated corridor (2-hour rated). How should this wall be graphically represented on the plan to clearly indicate its fire-rating requirement?

options.text: Solid thick line, same as any other interior partition, which does not indicate fire rating
Thick line with horizontal hatching or dashed pattern, labeled '2-HR FIR' (2-hour fire-rated)
Dashed line with no special marking; fire rating is shown only in specifications, not graphically, which is incorrect
Red line (colored); color indicates fire rating on plans, which is not a standard practice

rationale.a: Incorrect—solid line without marking does not distinguish fire-rated from standard partition.
rationale.c: Incorrect—fire rating should be graphically evident on plans (hatching/dashing + label), not only in specs.
rationale.d: Incorrect—color coding is not standard in CAD-based or printed architectural plans (though some offices may use it internally).
rationale.correct: Fire-rated walls are represented with a distinctive graphic—typically horizontal hatching or a dashed line pattern—and labeled with the fire-rating requirement (e.g., '2-HR FIR', '4-HR FIR'). This makes clear to contractors that the wall requires special assembly and testing, not just standard framing.
rationale.takeaway: Fire-rated walls = distinctive graphic (hatching or dashing) + text label (2-HR, 4-HR, etc.). This ensures contractor awareness and inspection compliance.

questions.code_citation: PD 1096 Section 505 (Plans—Fire-Rated Assembly Notation); PHILGBC/AIA Standards

questions.text: A floor plan shows a room labeled 'Office A: 5.0m × 4.0m = 20 m²' with dimensions marked. Are these dimensions measured as interior clear width/length or including wall thickness?

options.text: Including wall thickness (exterior face to exterior face), which is not standard for calculating room area
Interior clear (wall face to wall face inside the room), which is standard for room area calculation
From centerline to centerline of walls (structural convention), which is typically used for structural calculations rather than room area
Custom to each architect; no standard applies, although most follow established conventions for clarity

rationale.a: Incorrect—including wall thickness would overstate room area and is not standard.
rationale.c: Incorrect—centerline-to-centerline is used in structural drawing, not room dimension.
rationale.correct: Room dimensions are measured interior clear (face-to-face inside the room). C-C means centerline-to-centerline (structural). Wall thickness is NOT included in room area calculation unless explicitly noted. This is the standard practice per ISO 1091 and Philippine architectural convention.
rationale.takeaway: Room dimensions = interior clear (face-to-face inside). Wall thickness is shown in the wall graphic but not included in the dimension. Always clarify if structural walls are included (rare, but sometimes noted).

questions.text: A floor plan shows an accessible bathroom with a toilet stall layout. Which of the following is a mandatory measurement that must be clearly dimensioned on the plan per BP 344?

options.text: The clear floor space (minimum 1.5m diameter wheelchair turning circle)
The toilet seat height (0.4–0.45m), which ensures accessibility for individuals with mobility impairments
The sink depth (0.3m typical), allowing for adequate space for wheelchair users to approach and use the sink comfortably
The mirror mounting height (1.2m AFF), ensuring visibility for all users, including those in wheelchairs

rationale.b: Incorrect—toilet height is a fixture specification, not a critical plan dimension for accessibility review.
rationale.c: Incorrect—sink depth is standard; not a critical accessible dimension.
rationale.d: Incorrect—mirror height is accessibility detail but not the primary plan dimension.
rationale.correct: BP 344 (Accessibility Law) requires accessible bathrooms to provide a 1.5m diameter clear floor space for wheelchair maneuvering. This dimension must be explicitly shown on plans to verify compliance during review. Other measurements (toilet height, sink depth) are standard fixtures; the turning circle is the critical dimension that determines accessibility.
rationale.takeaway: Accessible bathrooms on plans must clearly show the 1.5m (minimum) clear floor space for wheelchair turning. This is the key dimension for BP 344 compliance verification.

questions.text: On a floor plan, a staircase is shown with tread lines and an arrow labeled 'UP'. This convention indicates:

options.text: The direction occupants ascend when using the stair
The stair location only; arrow direction is arbitrary
The staircase serves an upper floor; arrow shows vertical travel direction
The fire egress route; arrows show emergency exit direction

rationale.b: Incorrect—arrow direction is NOT arbitrary; it specifically shows vertical travel direction.
rationale.c: Partially correct (serves upper floor), but the primary purpose of the arrow is direction notation, not just location.
rationale.d: Incorrect—stair arrows show vertical direction, not fire egress route (though stairs ARE egress; the arrow is not specifically marking them as such).
rationale.correct: Stair convention: Tread lines (parallel lines showing each step) with 'UP' or 'DN' arrow clearly indicate direction of ascent/descent. This is critical for orientation—looking at a plan, you know immediately whether the stair goes up or down from that floor level.
rationale.takeaway: Stairs on plan: tread lines + 'UP'/'DN' arrow. UP = ascending this floor to the next; DN = descending to the floor below. Essential for plan orientation.

questions.text: In architectural floor plan conventions, at what height above finished floor (AFF) is a horizontal slice typically taken to create a floor plan?

options.text: 0.5 m AFF, which is too low to capture standard window openings
1.0 m AFF, a common height for capturing door and window openings
2.0 m AFF, which is too high and would miss most interior features

rationale.a: Incorrect—0.5 m is too low; would show furniture and base details.
rationale.b: Incorrect—1.0 m is close but slightly low; does not reliably capture all door heads.
rationale.d: Incorrect—2.0 m is too high; may miss some window sills and would not capture some door configurations.
rationale.correct: Floor plans are drawn as a horizontal section at 1.2–1.5 m AFF. This height cuts through door/window openings, captures room configuration, and avoids ceiling elements. This is the ISO standard adopted in Philippine architectural practice.
rationale.takeaway: Standard plan cut = 1.2–1.5 m AFF. This height reliably captures doors and windows while showing clear spatial organization.

questions.text: On a floor plan, the maximum travel distance from any point in an occupied space to the nearest exit is marked as 45 meters. Does this comply with NBC egress requirements?

options.text: Yes—45m is the maximum allowed travel distance for all occupancy types, which is a misinterpretation
No—maximum travel distance is 30m regardless of occupancy, which is incorrect
Yes, if the space is served by a single exit; if two exits are present, travel distance can extend to 60m, which is a common misconception
Depends on occupancy type and number of exits; 45m is maximum for single exit, but 60m allowed with two exits

rationale.a: Incorrect—travel distance varies by number of exits and occupancy type.
rationale.b: Incorrect—30m is not the standard; 45m/60m is correct.
rationale.c: Partially correct (60m with two exits) but wrong on single exit (should be 45m, not allowing 45m as insufficient).
rationale.correct: PD 1096 Rule IV Section 1005 (Means of Egress—Travel Distance) specifies: Travel distance to nearest exit = 45m maximum (single exit scenario). If two independent exits are provided from the space, travel distance can extend to 60m. This is the fundamental life-safety trade-off: more exits = more distance allowed.
rationale.takeaway: Egress travel distance = 45m (one exit) or 60m (two exits). Plans must mark travel distance and confirm compliance before BPBD approval.

questions.text: On an architectural floor plan, how is a door opening conventionally represented?

options.text: A solid rectangle at the location of the door frame, indicating the structural boundary
A line representing the door frame with a swing arc showing 90° opening direction
A double line showing both sides of the door panel, providing a detailed view
A dashed line indicating the door's interior position when closed, used for clarity

rationale.a: Incorrect—a solid rectangle shows a solid wall, not a door opening.
rationale.c: Incorrect—double line is used for some window representations, not standard for doors.
rationale.d: Incorrect—dashed lines show walls or hidden elements; door swings are solid arcs.
rationale.correct: Door convention: A line shows the door frame location; a 90° arc drawn from the hinge shows the swing direction (opening away from the room for egress, typically). The arc indicates which side of the door is the hinge and clarifies opening direction for code review (egress swing, accessible approach, etc.).
rationale.takeaway: Door = line (frame) + 90° arc (swing direction). The arc always points away from the room the door serves.

questions.text: A floor plan shows a rectangular room with dimensions marked as 'C-C 3.5m × 4.0m' and area labeled '14 m²'. The exterior wall thickness is 0.3m. What is the likely intention of the 'C-C' notation?

options.text: Center-to-center (wall centerline to centerline), used for structural coordination
Clear-to-clear (interior face-to-face), the standard room dimension, ensuring accurate space planning
Curved corner (indicating rounded interior corners), which may be used for aesthetic purposes or to meet specific design requirements
Construction center (indicating the building's geometric center), often used in complex layouts for precise alignment

rationale.b: Partially correct interpretation—if C-C meant clear-to-clear, then 3.5 × 4.0 = 14 m² is correct. However, architectural convention is more commonly 'C-C interior' or 'clear', not 'C-C' which is structural.
rationale.c: Incorrect—C-C does not indicate curved corners.
rationale.correct: C-C typically means center-to-center (wall centerline to centerline), which is a structural/dimensional convention. However, for room areas, the calculation should be interior face-to-face (clear interior). The notation 'C-C' is sometimes used ambiguously in Philippine practice—it can mean centerline-to-centerline (structural) or clear-to-clear (architectural). In this context, 14 m² does not equal 3.5 × 4.0 if those are C-C structural dimensions (would be ~14.56 m² with 0.3m walls). The question tests awareness of dimensional notation ambiguity.
rationale.takeaway: C-C notation is ambiguous in architectural drawings. Clarify: centerline-to-centerline (structural) vs. clear interior (room area). For room dimensions, interior face-to-face is standard. Always confirm notation in drawing set general notes.

questions.text: On a floor plan, diagonal hatching pattern (45° lines) across a solid area typically indicates:

options.text: A wall area; usually concrete or masonry
A void or empty space (like a room) indicating areas that are open and unobstructed
Fire-rated assembly requiring specific materials and construction methods per building code
Existing condition to remain (no demolition) as documented in the as-built survey drawings

rationale.b: Incorrect—blank/white space shows voids; hatching shows solid.
rationale.c: Incorrect—fire-rated walls are shown with horizontal hatching or a dashed line with 'FIR' notation, not diagonal.
rationale.d: Incorrect—'existing to remain' is shown with cross-hatching or notation, not simple diagonal.
rationale.correct: Diagonal hatching (45°) is the universal convention for solid material—concrete, masonry, structural elements. Blank (white) space indicates voids (rooms, corridors). This distinguishes between solid and void in a simple visual language.
rationale.takeaway: Diagonal hatching (45°) = solid material (concrete, masonry). Blank = void (room, air space). Horizontal hatching = fire-rated.
